HubSpot's Context Home is designed to hold business, team, and customer context for AI. That makes policy time a first-class concern. If a sales methodology or product statement changes, every agent, project, workflow, and recommendation depending on it may need review.

An action is current only when all four clocks are within their allowed windows.

The Context Freshness Budget

Assign each action a maximum tolerated age for each clock.

Draft an internal account brief

Prioritize a sales follow-up

Send a renewal commitment

Current transition policy

Escalate a critical ticket

Current escalation policy

These are examples, not universal thresholds. The business owner should set the budget based on consequence, reversibility, and update behavior.

The gate can be expressed plainly:

if event_age > event_budget: refresh evidence
if capture_lag > capture_budget: wait or query the source
if interpretation_age > interpretation_budget: recompute
if policy_version != current_policy: re-evaluate
if any required clock is unknown: ask, narrow, or stop

This is more useful than a single "data freshness" score because it identifies which kind of staleness must be repaired.

Context Freshness Budget infographic

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

At 14:00, a customer meets with an account executive. During the call, the customer says procurement cannot approve the proposed term. The call ends at 14:30.

At 14:32, the calendar and meeting activity sync to HubSpot. At 14:38, the transcript arrives. At 14:42, a summary identifies "strong interest" because the customer praised the product. The deal score increases. At 14:45, a prospecting workflow prepares a follow-up that assumes the contract can close this week.

At 14:46, the account executive adds a note: "Do not send commercial follow-up. Legal review required."

A current-record view may show a meeting, a positive summary, and a high score. A four-clock view sees:

  • the procurement objection occurred before the positive score was calculated.
  • the decisive transcript arrived six minutes after the activity shell.
  • the summary extracted enthusiasm but missed the gating condition.
  • the current sales rule says a legal objection blocks automated commercial outreach.

The safe response is not to delete the score or ignore AI. It is to recompute the interpretation using the complete evidence, apply the current policy, and stop the external message.

Use HubSpot history as evidence, not decoration

HubSpot provides property history with value, date, and source information. Current documentation also describes exportable property history and, for individual records, the ability to inspect which user or tool changed a value. Agent-created changes can identify the agent in the source when the relevant feature is enabled.

That history supports three controls:

  1. distinguish a human edit, workflow, import, integration, and agent action.
  2. determine whether a late update overwrote a later business event.
  3. reconstruct a previous value when the current interpretation is wrong.

History has limits. HubSpot documents revision limits that vary by object type. A high-consequence audit trail may need an external event store or warehouse with longer retention. The CRM history can be an important source without being the entire evidence system.

Separate observed, derived, and governed fields

The easiest freshness mistake is treating every property as the same kind of fact.

Classify important context into three categories:

Call occurred, email delivered, ticket opened

Reconcile with source event

Deal score, intent label, churn risk, summary

Recompute from current evidence

Contactable, approved discount, service entitlement

Re-evaluate against current policy and authority

An observed event can remain historically true forever. A derived conclusion may decay quickly. A governed permission may be revoked instantly.

Do not give all three one generic "last updated" rule.

Failure modes to test before trusting automation

Create synthetic scenarios that force the clocks apart:

  1. A transcript arrives after a workflow evaluates the meeting.
  2. An older integration event retries after a human correction.
  3. A score remains high after the underlying source becomes stale.
  4. A sales policy changes while an agent run is queued.
  5. A property update has a current timestamp but came from an unauthorized source.
  6. An associated ticket contains a blocker that the deal summary did not retrieve.
  7. An agent updates a record and then reads its own write as independent evidence.

For each scenario, verify the expected response: refresh, recompute, ask, narrow, escalate, or stop.

Metrics that reveal semantic staleness

Track the distance between the four clocks:

  • median and maximum event-to-capture lag by source;
  • percentage of derived fields outside their interpretation budget;
  • actions blocked by an outdated policy version;
  • late events that overwrote a newer value;
  • summaries regenerated after decisive evidence arrived;
  • agent actions reversed because context was incomplete;
  • customer-facing messages produced before all critical sources synchronized;
  • time from policy change to every dependent workflow and agent being retested.

The goal is not zero lag. The goal is to know which lag is acceptable for which decision.

A self-updating CRM still needs a theory of time

Automatic activity capture is valuable. It reduces missing history and gives HubSpot AI more of the customer journey to work with. The stronger the automation becomes, the more important it is to distinguish collection from interpretation and interpretation from permission.

The CRM should not merely know what changed most recently. It should know when the business event happened, when the evidence arrived, when its meaning was evaluated, and which policy governed the proposed action.

That is how a self-updating CRM becomes a trustworthy context foundation rather than a faster way to circulate the wrong story.

items.title: Your AI Context Is Becoming a Second CRM. Govern It Like One.
items.author: Pratik Thakker
items.content:
On September 16, 2026, HubSpot introduced Context Home as part of its Fall Spotlight release. The product idea is compelling: put the business, team, and customer knowledge used by AI in one place, then let Breeze Assistant and agents use that shared understanding across the platform.

That also creates a new system of record.

It may not look like a CRM. It contains guidelines, methodologies, product descriptions, user preferences, files, and memories rather than contacts and deals. Yet it can shape customer messages, agent configurations, recommendations, and record-changing actions. If it is wrong, the error can spread far beyond one field.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

The control I recommend is a : six explicit rules that determine why shared AI context exists, who owns it, where it applies, what wins during conflict, when it expires, and how changes are reviewed.

Context is not another prompt library

HubSpot's current documentation distinguishes two information layers:

  • is foundational information about the business that can be applied across multiple HubSpot AI tools.
  • are collections manually attached to particular projects or agents for specific use cases.

That is an important architectural distinction. A company description, brand guideline, product catalog, sales methodology, user profile, and service escalation policy do not have the same audience or consequence.

If they are all treated as interchangeable prompt material, teams will eventually create one of three failures:

  1. Global context is too generic. It becomes safe but useless.
  2. Global context is too specific. A rule for one team silently affects another.
  3. Local context contradicts global context. The AI receives two plausible instructions without a declared precedence rule.

The answer is not more prose. It is governance around the prose.

The six-clause Context Constitution

Every context item should carry six controls. These can live in a registry, document header, custom object, or external governance service. The storage choice matters less than making the rules explicit.

State the decision or behavior the context is allowed to influence.

"Our company serves mid-market and enterprise teams" is descriptive. "Prioritize companies with 200 to 2,000 employees for outbound prospecting" is an action rule. They should not share the same governance because the second can change who receives outreach.

A useful purpose field names both the allowed use and the excluded use:

{
  "context_id": "ctx_icp_2026_q3",
  "allowed_uses": ["prospect_research", "lead_prioritization"],
  "excluded_uses": ["service_entitlement", "credit_decision"]
}

Without purpose boundaries, reusable context becomes an invisible policy engine.

Record who is authorized to define the knowledge.

Marketing may own brand voice. Finance may own discount rules. Revenue operations may own lifecycle definitions. Legal may own approved disclosure language. A sales manager can suggest a pricing exception, but that does not make the manager the authority for pricing policy.

Authority should attach to a subject, not merely a job title. "Admin" proves system access. It does not prove business ownership.

Define which users, teams, projects, and agents may receive the context.

HubSpot's Context Home allows custom context to be entered as text or files, with visibility settings. Breeze projects also have access settings. Those controls should reflect business scope, not convenience.

A service escalation playbook may be appropriate for a customer agent but irrelevant to a content-generation project. A confidential pricing methodology may help a deal agent while being unsuitable for a broad marketing workspace.

Defaulting every context item to portal-wide access creates a larger and less observable decision surface.

Declare what happens when two context items disagree.

Consider these instructions:

  • Company context: "Never discount implementation services."
  • Sales project: "Strategic accounts may receive a 10 percent implementation discount."
  • Deal note: "Finance approved a one-time 12 percent exception."

The AI should not infer which instruction is more important from wording. The constitution should specify a hierarchy such as current signed exception, current policy, approved project instruction, user preference.

Precedence also needs a conflict response. If two sources at the same level disagree, the correct behavior may be to ask, narrow the action, or stop.

Give context an effective date, review date, and expiry behavior.

Brand principles may remain stable for a year. A campaign offer may expire Friday. A territory map can change monthly. A product limitation may change with a release.

An old context item is more dangerous than a missing one because it appears authoritative. Use explicit states:

Owner has not reconfirmed it

Use only for low-consequence drafting

Do not retrieve by default

Its validity window ended

Stop or request current context

"Last edited" is not enough. A document can remain correct without editing, and a newly edited document can still be wrong.

Preserve who changed the context, what changed, why it changed, and which outputs were tested.

HubSpot's AI documentation emphasizes access settings, sources, memories, and controls over data shared with AI. Those product controls are necessary. Enterprise teams also need a business review trail that answers:

  • Which customer-facing behaviors depend on this context?
  • Which tests were rerun after the change?
  • Who approved the new rule?
  • Can the previous version be reconstructed?
  • Which agents or projects must be revalidated?

The evidence belongs beside the context change, not in a separate chat that disappears from the decision path.

A worked HubSpot scenario

Imagine a company using shared context for Breeze Assistant, a prospecting agent, and a customer agent.

The portal-wide product description says the enterprise plan includes priority support. A service knowledge vault says priority support means a four-hour response. A sales project contains an older deck promising one-hour response. The CRM company record identifies the prospect as enterprise, but the signed order form uses a negotiated two-hour response.

All four statements may be traceable to legitimate sources. Only one should govern a customer commitment.

The Context Constitution resolves the path:

  1. the question concerns a contractual service commitment.
  2. the signed order form governs the individual customer; the service policy governs the default.
  3. the negotiated term is available to the service agent and deal project, not to unrelated marketing projects.
  4. signed customer terms override a sales deck and default policy.
  5. the current contract version is valid; the older deck is superseded.
  6. the response cites the contract source and records which context governed the answer.

The result is not simply a better response. It is an explainable response.

Context Constitution infographic

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Build the registry before the library grows

Start with a small register of high-impact context rather than cataloging every sentence in the portal.

Prioritize context that can change:

  • lead qualification or prioritization;
  • pricing or service commitments;
  • ticket routing and escalation;
  • compliance or consent behavior.

What stable identifier follows this item across versions?

Who is accountable for its meaning?

Who maintains it in HubSpot?

Which decisions may it influence?

Which users, projects, and agents may use it?

What evidence supports it?

What wins when it conflicts?

When must the owner reconfirm it?

Ask, narrow, escalate, or stop?

This register can begin outside HubSpot. The goal is not to build a large governance product before using Context Home. The goal is to prevent important knowledge from becoming anonymous, timeless, and universal.

Test context as a dependency

Teams test workflows and agents. They should also test the context those systems consume.

Create a compact suite of scenarios:

  1. Two sources disagree at different authority levels.
  2. A context item passes its review date.
  3. A project instruction conflicts with portal context.
  4. A user memory contains an outdated preference.
  5. A file is replaced but a knowledge vault still references the old version.
  6. A restricted context item is requested by an unauthorized project.
  7. A context change would alter an external message or CRM write.

The expected result must be defined before the test. "The response looked reasonable" is not a control.

Metrics that expose context debt

Track more than context completeness. A portal can be fully populated and still be poorly governed.

  • percentage of action-critical context with a named business owner;
  • percentage with a current review date;
  • retrievals of superseded or expired items;
  • conflicts between portal, project, memory, and record context;
  • outputs blocked because authority was unclear;
  • customer-facing corrections caused by stale context;
  • time from a business-policy change to every affected context update;
  • agent tests rerun after a context change.

These metrics separate "we added context" from "we can trust how context is used."

Context Home should become a control plane

HubSpot's release makes context visible as a first-class product layer. That is the opportunity.

If teams treat Context Home as a setup page, the shared knowledge will gradually become a second CRM without the controls of the first. If they treat it as a control plane, they can make business knowledge explicit, scoped, current, and reviewable before AI turns it into action.

The competitive advantage is not having the longest company description or the largest knowledge vault. It is knowing which context governs which decision, and being able to prove why.

Vested-interest disclosure: INSIDEA is linked because I lead the company and its work includes HubSpot, CRM, RevOps, automation, and AI services. The framework and recommendations in this article are independent analysis, not sponsored content.

items.title: Sovereignty. Somewhere Between a Border and a Login
items.author: Andrei Mochola
items.content:
Sovereignty is not fundamentally about where data is stored. It is about who retains the capacity to decide, govern, change, and ultimately survive without asking someone else for permission.

For the past few months I spent a surprising amount of time talking about sovereignty. Data sovereignty. Digital sovereignty. Cloud sovereignty. Sovereign infrastructure. Sovereign cloud. Sometimes the conversation becomes so specific that we start discussing where a server physically sits, who operates it, who owns the keys, which jurisdiction governs the provider, and what happens if something goes wrong. And certificates… don’t forget the certificates!

Quite often, we have these conversations on Microsoft Teams, Zoom or Google Meet. There is something almost about discussing technological independence through infrastructure operated by some of the world's most powerful technology companies.

It is not quite a contradiction. But it is certainly worth noticing. Because perhaps the problem begins with the way we understand sovereignty in the first place.

Sovereignty was never really about geography

The modern political concept of sovereignty is usually associated with territory, borders and the state. That association is so strong that it is easy to forget that .

Jean Bodin, writing in sixteenth-century France, described sovereignty as the highest and perpetual power of the commonwealth. His concern was not servers, borders or databases. It was the question of who ultimately has the authority to make decisions and establish the rules under which a political community exists.

Centuries later, the concept evolved through very different political traditions. Hobbes connected supreme authority with the problem of order and collective security. Later theories shifted the source of sovereignty toward the people, constitutions and institutions.

The details changed. The underlying question did not: And perhaps an even more important question follows: Who gets to decide when somebody else disagrees? That second question is where sovereignty becomes particularly interesting in the digital world.

A country can have a flag, a currency, a parliament, a constitution, internationally recognised borders and an army to protect them. But what happens when some of the infrastructure through which its economy, public administration, communications and essential services operate is controlled somewhere else? The territory remains sovereign. The dependency may not be.

From land to infrastructure

This is where the contemporary discussion about digital sovereignty becomes more interesting than a simple conversation about data localisation. Data sovereignty is often reduced to a question of location:

But location is only one layer of control. Here are few other things to consider:

  • Who operates the infrastructure?
  • Who controls the software?
  • Who controls the encryption keys?
  • Who can change the terms?
  • Who can discontinue the service?
  • Which country's laws apply to the provider?
  • Who has access to the supply chain?
  • Who can realistically replace the system if the relationship ends?

And, perhaps most importantly: Who can continue operating when circumstances change?

These questions point toward a broader conception of sovereignty. The European Commission now defines technology sovereignty in terms of Europe's ability to act independently in the digital world by developing and controlling key technologies, data and infrastructure while reducing reliance on non-EU providers.

That definition is revealing. It does not say that Europe should stop using foreign technology. It says that dependence matters. And there is a significant difference.

Dependence is not the opposite of sovereignty

No modern country is completely self-sufficient. Countries depend on one another for energy, raw materials, manufacturing, finance, telecommunications, transportation, medicine and technology. Modern economies are built on interdependence.

So the question cannot realistically be: Can we become completely independent? The more useful question is: Which dependencies are acceptable, and which dependencies become dangerous?

That distinction is important because sovereignty is sometimes presented as technological autarky: build everything yourself, own everything yourself, keep everything inside your borders. That is neither particularly realistic nor necessarily desirable.

A country may perfectly reasonably decide that it does not need to manufacture every processor, write every operating system or operate every cloud platform itself. But it may also decide that certain capabilities are too important to be entirely dependent on somebody else's goodwill.

Sovereignty, then, begins to look less like isolation and more like . The ability to say yes. And equally, the ability to say no. And, critically, the ability to change your mind. Sounds like basic freedoms, doesn’t it?

This is where digital sovereignty becomes philosophically awkward. Suppose a government stores sensitive information inside its own country. The data centre is physically located there. The employees operating it are local. The contracts are governed by local law. It sounds sovereign.

But perhaps the infrastructure depends on foreign software. Or foreign hardware (where the chip comes from?). Or foreign cloud management tools. Or foreign security technologies. Or foreign telecommunications equipment. Or a foreign platform or API that ultimately controls a critical dependency somewhere further down the stack.

Where, then, does sovereignty begin? And where does it end? There may be no clean answer.

A quick review of the latest academic literature on digital sovereignty makes precisely this problem visible: the concept is used by different actors in different ways, and scholars increasingly question whether “digital sovereignty” represents a genuine extension of sovereignty or a stretching of an older political concept to fit a new technological environment.

The term itself is applied to multiple actors and values, rather than referring exclusively to states. That matters because perhaps we have been asking the wrong question.

Instead of asking: “Is this system sovereign?” we might need to ask: “Sovereign in what sense?”

  • Technological sovereignty?
  • And who is the subject of that sovereignty?

The answer may be different in every case, I’m afraid.

Sovereignty is also a capacity

There is another way of looking at this. Sovereignty may not mean possessing everything. It may mean retaining sufficient  (Braun). A sovereign state does not necessarily manufacture every product consumed by its citizens. It does not need to own every road, every factory or every computer.

But if a dependency becomes so fundamental that the state cannot act without another actor's permission, the character of that relationship changes.

This is why infrastructure matters. Infrastructure is not neutral. It creates possibilities and constraints. A railway determines how goods can move. An electricity grid determines what can operate. A telecommunications network determines how people communicate. Financial infrastructure determines how transactions can occur.

Digital infrastructure increasingly does the same. Cloud platforms, identity systems, collaboration tools, operating systems, payment networks, app stores and data infrastructures are not merely convenient pieces of technology. They are becoming part of the environment in which institutions exercise power. And that brings us back to platforms.

In an earlier article, I explored the idea of the platform as a kind of social contract: a space where governance, rules and trust become inseparable from the technology itself. Sovereignty takes that argument one level higher.

The Teams (Zoom, Meet etc.) paradox

Which brings us back to Teams & Co. There is nothing inherently wrong with using Microsoft Teams (or any other such tool) to discuss digital sovereignty. That would be taking the argument too far. Interdependence is normal. Global technology ecosystems are normal. And foreign technology is not automatically a sovereignty problem.

But the irony is useful. We can spend an hour discussing how to protect our digital autonomy while relying on infrastructure whose ownership, governance, legal exposure and economic value sit partly outside our own jurisdiction.

The same phenomenon appears everywhere. We want data sovereignty, but use globally dominant platforms to move and process the data. We want technological autonomy, but depend on global supply chains. We want open standards, but build workflows around proprietary ecosystems. We want resilience, but sometimes concentrate critical functions in a handful of providers.

This is not hypocrisy. It is something more interesting. It is the schizophrenia of digital sovereignty: the gap between the control we increasingly want and the dependencies we have already built our digital lives around. And that gap is precisely where the real conversation begins.

From sovereignty to choice

Perhaps digital sovereignty should therefore not be understood as the digital equivalent of building a wall around a country. It is better understood as a question of . Can an institution understand its dependencies? Can it govern them? Can it move between providers? Can it preserve access to its data? Can it operate when a supplier fails? Can it resist unwanted external interference? Can it maintain critical capabilities under changing political or economic circumstances?

And can it make these choices without having to rebuild its entire digital existence from scratch?

If the answer is yes, there may be a meaningful degree of sovereignty. If the answer is no, storing the data in the right country may provide only a comforting illusion of control. This is why sovereignty has become such an important concept in technology. Not because the internet abolished borders. It didn't. But because it created something much more complicated: a world in which borders remain political, while dependencies increasingly run through infrastructure that does not respect them.

The next question, then, is unavoidable. If sovereignty once depended on controlling territory, what happens when some of the most important territory in our lives is no longer land at all?

It is infrastructure. And infrastructure, unlike territory, can be rented. That may be where the story really begins.

Further Reading and Conceptual References

  •  - (capacity to control our present and our future in a digital environment).
  • Berman (Shiff Berman) P. (ed.) - The Oxford Handbook of Global Legal Pluralism (how state-driven digital sovereignty collides with overlapping, non-state legal and normative systems in cyberspace.)
  • - Six Books of the Commonwealth (the classical foundation for understanding sovereignty as supreme political authority).
  • - Is digital sovereignty normatively desirable? (sovereignty through institutions, rules and practices).
  • - What does the concept of sovereignty mean for digital technologies? (sovereignty through technological capability, innovation and control).
  • -  (sovereignty, political authority and the preservation of collective order).
  • - Data sovereignty: A review (data sovereignty across individual, collective and national dimensions)
  • - Attributes of Digital Sovereignty: A Conceptual Framework (political power and control of digital networks, infrastructure, and data)

items.title: UX Metrics That Show the Business Impact of Product Design
items.author: Saurabh Srivastava
items.content:
In what ways does design contribute to both user satisfaction and business outcomes?

As Product Designers, we grapple with a challenge: our inherent creativity.

The creative nature inherent in Product Designers places us in a delicate position. Businesses, often prioritize practicality over creativity and we all have experienced that sometime in our career. Despite this contrast, we find ourselves, as Product Designers, contributing within a business framework. Questions arise about our purpose: What is our role here? How do we validate our presence? And, most importantly, how do we derive significance from our work? These questions revolve not around existential pondering but around understanding how we can quantify the beneficial impact of our creative efforts on the business.

This stands in contrast to product key performance indicators (KPIs) like return on investment, revenue growth, revenue per client, and profit margin, which are vital for assessing product performance and overall business impact.

So, is everything about how we can bring/show business impact / about success numbers?

Yes, precisely. It’s not solely about creativity; it’s about delivering tangible value when working for a business.

Using the right set of UX metrics serves to clarify the distinct advantages that Product Designers contribute to a business in term of metrics. It enables businesses to attain an unbiased, objective viewpoint on their products from the perspective of their customers, emphasizing the concrete value derived from impactful design.

Unfortunately, there is no universal set of metrics that work for every project. That’s why the first thing we need to do when choosing metrics is to learn what metrics can bring a significant impact on your business/project bottom line.

What are UX design metrics?

(although sometimes it’s really hard to distinguish UX metrics from marketing/product metrics).

  • — How users interact with the product
  • — How users perceive the product

User perception and interaction can be influenced by context and surroundings. Consequently, analyzing behavioral or attitudinal metrics in isolation may not offer an accurate representation of information. As a designer, it is vital to acknowledge that a thorough analysis necessitates the simultaneous consideration of both behavioral and attitudinal metrics. If attitudinal and behavioral metrics align, they become noteworthy metrics for consideration. However, in the presence of discrepancies, qualitative research becomes essential to uncover the actual reasons behind the disparity.

Let’s delve into a comprehensive discussion about behavioral and attitudinal metrics.

Behavioral metrics — How users interact with the product

How many users complete a task and how long it took them? Behavioral metrics tell you how users interact with your product and what problems they face along the way. Most behavioral metrics mentioned below are relevant to the usability ()

The time that a user spends doing a particular task. Works perfectly where the user’s goal is to get something done as efficiently as possible.

an absolute number (seconds, minutes, hours)

Time on Task = Time Task Completed — Time Task Started

B. Average session length

The average time users spend on your product. Depending on your product goal, these metrics can be considered positive or negative depending on the use case

The dropout rate is the ratio between the number of users who left the task incomplete vs the total number of users who attempted the task.

Dropout rate = ( user left the task / total number of users) X100%

The error rate (UER) is the number of times a user makes a mistake while completing a task.

Eg: Users making mistakes while filling out the

Error Rate = Number of Errors / Total Number of Actions

The percentage of users who can complete a task

Task Success Rate = Number of Successful Completions / Total Number of Attempts

This metric measures the percentage of users who take a desired action.

It can indicate how well the design supports the user’s goals.

Conversion Rate = (Number of Conversions / Total Number of Users) x 100%

Attitudinal metrics — How users perceive the product

This is a perspective metric, which needs to be backed by qualitative research.

How do they find the task overly complex to complete? Did they feel confident using the system?

  • S_atisfaction_ (Do your users enjoy your product?),
  • (Do your users trust your service?), and
  • (Do your users plan to use your service again?)

A. Daily/Monthly Active Users (DAU/MAU)

How many people use a product on a daily/weekly/monthly basis? This number also tells you about retention.

The DAU/MAU ratio, also known as stickiness, is the proportion of monthly active users that engage with your product every day

B. Net Promoter Score (NPS)

Net Promoter Score (NPS) is a simple survey with only one question. You ask your users, “How likely is it that you would recommend our product to a friend or colleague on a scale from 1 to 10?”. Net Promoter Score scale with 3 user groups: (who can damage your brand and impede growth through negative word-of-mouth), (who are vulnerable to competitive offerings), and (who will keep buying and fuel growth by referring others.).

The Net Promoter Score (NPS) offers a swift means of gathering user feedback with its single-question format. However, its simplicity comes with limitations — lack of customization and the challenge of comprehending the rationale behind specific scores, especially without follow-up questions. NPS requires a large sample size. There are other cons that users could perceive the question differently based on their language and cultural background. Survey timing is critical; for example, soliciting feedback immediately after a user opens an app for the first time or during the completion of a significant task may increase the likelihood of negative responses or biased response

C. Customer Satisfaction (CSAT)

Measuring: Satisfaction, Loyalty

CSAT score is the percentage of satisfied and very satisfied users in all the respondents.

The problem with this type of method is that not all users are willing to spend their time filling out the survey nor do they feel what they are inputting. What is the user’s mood at the time of the survey, and what time survey is asked during the experience eg if the survey has been asked just after opening the app for the first time, the possibility of getting negative feedback is very high

User retention rate is the percentage of users who have stayed with you over a given period. To calculate the user retention rate, you need to subtract the number of acquired users throughout a period from the number of users at the end of the period and then divide it by the number of users at the beginning of the period.

, it’s important to highlight that revenue-generating products, despite meeting business criteria, may encounter an unexpected decline in their customer base if they lack crucial UX insights

Finally, it depends on your project’s and team’s particular needs and which metrics you choose to put into action.

items.title: How Believable is Google's New 'Live Avatar' Capability?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Google has synthesized "expressive face-to-face experiences" for its speech agent Gemini 3.8 Live. They're now offering a Live Avatar "with precise lip-syncing, natural expressions, and fluid turn-taking" for Google Enterprise accounts wanting "engaging customer service" or for offering interactive walkthroughs. (Check out the not-creepy-at-all video in Google's announcement.) 

"Though Google will offer a library of preset avatars for customers to choose from, it will also allow organizations to create their own," notes The Verge. (See some examples from the YouTube channel "AI with Surya".) 

But even without the visualization of the avatar, "I was never able to shake the feeling that these conversations with computers never feel like a real conversation," argues the blog Android Police. Conversing with just the Ai-generated audio, "At best, they feel like talking to a phone representative or someone from tech support. We turn to them when we have a problem, and they help us through it..."

GPT-Live, and Gemini Live right behind it, skip that whole relay race. Instead of translating your voice to text and back to voice, the model works with raw audio the entire way through (what it hears and what it says) inside the same system, with nothing translated in between. That sounds like a small plumbing detail, but it's the whole story. Cutting out the text step lets these models respond in a fraction of a second instead of the pause we've learned to expect, and it lets them hear things text can never carry: tone, hesitation, whether you're annoyed or joking... 

I was hoping to be surprised by how natural the conversation felt. Instead, I came out with a deeper appreciation for every human I've ever talked to. Even the boring ones... I spoke, it spoke back. I spoke faster, it answered faster. Then I switched to a different language, and it switched along with me. Even switching between languages several times during the same sentence didn't stump it. The most impressive moment happened when I asked it what "T-O-P-G-3-3-K" spelled out, and it immediately came back with, "You are spelling the word Top Geek, but using a 3 to represent a reversed E...." 

 Although it felt fast and responsive, at no point did it feel like talking to another human being... What Gemini couldn't replicate, because it was never built to replicate it, is human connection.... I'm sure I'm not telling you something you don't already know, but somehow talking naturally to an LLM amplifies the feeling that there is no one on the other side of the line. It might flow like a phone call, but it doesn't feel like one. 

MrBrklyn (Slashdot reader #4,775) says he discussed "why mainstream media avoids reporting on screen dependency" with Gemini, and eventually convinced Gemini to respond that it's just "another tool built by the same tech giants to make sure you rely on their system to tell you what to think, how to talk, and what is real."

items.title: How inDrive Automated UI Testing for Dynamic Screens with AI
items.author: inDrive.Tech
items.content:
The GeoWay team in inDrive’s Geo cluster added an AI-powered analysis layer to its existing UI tests to handle screens where visual content changes from one run to another. The main use case is maps: route geometry, camera position, and pin placement can all vary on iOS and Android even when the screen is working exactly as expected.

Authors: Alexey Sumin and Oleg Anisimov, QA Engineers at inDrive

A map can look noticeably different from one mobile E2E test run to another and still be completely correct. The camera may shift, the route may take a slightly different shape, or a pin may move a few pixels. A person can usually look at the screen and tell immediately whether something is wrong. A pixel-by-pixel comparison cannot.

This was a recurring problem for our GeoWay team, especially in tests involving the map layer. Many of our scenarios depend on routes, pickup and destination points, navigation, vehicle positions, and other visual elements on the map. Appium is useful when you can check the presence or state of a specific UI element, but in our case it sees the map as a single layer rather than a set of elements with individual locators.

That means checking that a route exists is not enough. We also need to know whether it connects the right points, whether its geometry makes sense, and whether the screen looks correct as a whole. We had been using a pixel comparer for this, but it produced a lot of noise. A change to a font, icon, margin, or surrounding layout could slightly move the map and push the visual diff over the threshold even though nothing was actually broken.

Our original setup was fairly standard for visual regression testing. The project stores a golden screenshot, and during a test run the pixel comparer takes a new screenshot and calculates the difference between the two. If the diff stays below a configured threshold, the check passes.

This works well for stable interfaces. Maps are different. The camera may shift slightly, the zoom level can change, data outside the area we care about can affect the layout, and a routing provider may return different but equally valid geometry.

In one of our tests, for example, the comparer reported an 11.24% difference against a 5% threshold, although the route itself was correct.

There was no useful universal threshold we could set. Make it too strict and valid tests fail constantly. Make it too loose, and you risk missing a real issue. So the test report kept filling up with red cases that someone still had to inspect manually.

The pixel comparer was useful as a first filter, but it often could not make the final decision.

We kept the existing comparison logic and added another step only for ambiguous cases. We called it AI Judge.

The model is not involved in every test. Most checks still end with ordinary deterministic logic. AI Judge is called only when the pixel difference is too large for the normal threshold but still small enough that we consider the result worth analysing rather than rejecting outright.

  1. Run the UI test and take a screenshot.
  2. Compare it with the golden screenshot.
  3. If the diff is within the normal threshold, pass the test.
  4. If it is above that threshold, check a second limit configured for AI Judge.
  5. If the diff is within that range, send the expected and actual screenshots to the model. If it is above the upper limit, fail the test immediately.
  6. AI Judge checks the screenshots against the expectations defined for that specific test and returns pass or fail.

The limits are configurable per test. A relatively dynamic case might allow AI Judge to inspect differences of up to 40%, while a more stable screen can use a much lower boundary.

The important part is what we ask the model. We do not send a generic prompt such as “Are these screenshots similar?” Instead, each test describes what actually matters. For a route, that may mean checking that it is continuous, connects the right points, and shows the expected icons.

This changes the task from visual similarity to a much narrower question: does the actual screen still satisfy the test expectations?

If it does, AI Judge can rescue the test. We mark those cases separately so we can track them and review a sample manually. The model also returns a confidence score, and we define the minimum confidence we are willing to accept. If it finds a problem or is not confident enough, the test stays red.

The goal here is not to make the dashboard greener. It is to remove failures that are clearly noise without hiding real defects.

What happened with the 11.24% diff?

The earlier example is a good illustration. The routing provider returned slightly different geometry, so the pixel comparer rejected the screenshot at 11.24%. The route still connected the correct points and was functionally valid.

AI Judge checked the actual test expectations and passed it. Previously, a tester would have opened the report, looked at the screenshots, and reached the same conclusion manually.

This is essentially the role we wanted AI Judge to play. It does not replace Appium or visual regression testing. It handles a narrow class of cases where the deterministic check can see that something changed but cannot tell whether the change matters.

What changed in real runs?

We compared two recent nightly runs, one without AI Judge and one with it.

The number of failing tests went from 47 to 8 in those two runs. On iOS, failures dropped from 15 to 4; on Android, from 32 to 4.

We do not treat this as a permanent performance metric. The composition and total number of tests change between runs, so a single comparison can be misleading. What matters more is what disappeared from the report: many of the cases removed by AI Judge were tests that previously reached manual review and were then confirmed to be valid anyway.

The result is less noise. A red test is now more likely to be something worth opening.

The Bigger Benefit: Automating tests we used to run manually.

Reducing false failures was useful, but it was not the main reason we built this.

Navigation scenarios were much more interesting. Because the route comes from an external provider, its exact geometry cannot be fixed ahead of time. A completely correct route may still differ significantly from the baseline screenshot, which makes these tests awkward to automate with a normal pixel comparer.

Before AI Judge, some of these cases simply were not worth automating.

In one regression suite of around 120 test cases, all 120 previously required manual execution. With the new approach, we were able to automate roughly 100 of them, leaving about 20 for manual testing. The team estimates that this saves around two hours of manual work per regression cycle, although the exact number varies by run.

For us, this is the strongest argument for the approach. AI Judge is not just cleaning up reports. It makes automation practical for scenarios where screenshot-based testing had previously been too unstable.

The model cost turned out to be almost irrelevant.

We initially used GPT-5.4-mini and later moved AI Judge to GPT-5.6 Luna. In our tests, Luna performed better at analysing the screenshots while remaining cheap enough that model cost was not really a factor in the decision.

In recent runs, AI Judge processed 155,929 input tokens and 16,599 output tokens for iOS, and 83,187 input tokens and 30,118 output tokens for Android. Based on the pricing we used for the calculation in the project, that came to approximately $0.051 for iOS and $0.053 for Android, or around $0.104 in total.

Usage changes from run to run, so we do not treat those numbers as a fixed average. The useful conclusion is simpler: one regression run costs us a few cents, while manually checking noisy failures costs considerably more in engineering time.

We also track token usage directly in the test report so we can see how that changes as the test suite grows.

Prompt quality mattered more than we expected.

Once a model can change the final status of a test, false passes become the obvious risk. During the first month, we therefore kept manual review in place and regularly checked AI Judge decisions.

We found one questionable green result during that period. It was not an actual product bug, but according to our own expectations, the model should have been stricter.

What we saw more often was a different problem: the prompt itself was incomplete.

If we forgot to describe something important, the model could make a reasonable decision based on the information we had given it. The mistake was not necessarily in the image analysis. We had simply left part of the specification out.

That changed how we think about prompts. They are now effectively part of the test code. If the route must connect points A and B, that needs to be stated. If color matters, we need to say so. If an icon should be in a particular state, that condition belongs in the expectations as well.

We now review these prompts much like regular assertions. In practice, incomplete expectations have caused us more trouble than systematic image-recognition errors.

Automating reference screenshot updates as well.

There is another piece of automation in the same nightly screenshot workflow, although technically it is separate from AI Judge.

AI Judge decides whether a test result is valid. A second workflow helps us deal with reference screenshots when they genuinely need to be updated. Alexey worked on AI Judge, while Oleg implemented this part.

Previously, someone had to find the right image in a large report, download it, add it to the repository, and open a pull request manually.

Now, after every nightly run, an n8n workflow sends the results to Slack. The message includes the Android and iOS failures, the reason for each failure, a link to the report, and the relevant screenshots.

If a screenshot should become the new reference, the tester selects it and clicks Update. The workflow then creates a GitHub pull request with the selected images automatically.

The two automations solve different problems around the same workflow: AI Judge helps us decide whether a visual difference is actually a bug, while the bot removes some of the repetitive work involved in maintaining reference screenshots.

A few rules emerged after running this in the regression pipeline for several weeks.

We still prefer deterministic checks whenever they are enough. There is no reason to call a model if the pixel comparer can already give us a clear answer. AI is useful only in the ambiguous middle ground where understanding the content of the screen matters.

Keeping the task narrow also helps. AI Judge does not explore the product, generate the test, or decide how the application should behave. It evaluates one known state against a set of explicit expectations. That makes its decisions easier to understand and easier to review.

We are also conservative with confidence. If the model is not confident enough, the test stays red. And even after launch, we continue reviewing real regression runs rather than assuming that a good result on a test dataset is enough.

The problem we solved is not unique to GeoWay. Any mobile team working with maps, canvas-based interfaces, dynamic content, or third-party visual components can run into the same limitation: the screen is valid, but it differs too much from the reference image for simple pixel comparison.

We are now looking at whether AI Judge can become a reusable module and have already discussed the approach with other inDrive teams working on geo-related functionality. There are also smaller improvements we can make around the workflow. For example, the nightly report could distinguish a brand-new failure from one that has been appearing for days. AI could eventually suggest reference screenshot updates and prepare the pull request, leaving the final approval to a person.

The key point is that we did not rebuild the testing stack around AI. Appium, the pixel comparer, and the existing thresholds are still there. We added the model only at the point where deterministic checks stop being able to tell us whether a visual difference actually matters.

For our team, that turned out to be a small but useful addition to the pipeline. The model is not deciding how the application should work. It is helping us answer a much more practical question:

Is this visual difference acceptable, or is it a bug?

Special thanks to Karim Azab, GeoWay Tech Lead, for supporting the team while we worked on this automation, and to Vlad Ryzhkov. AI Judge grew out of Vlad’s earlier work on a workflow that analysed localization from screenshots; we adapted the same general idea for dynamic geo scenarios.

items.title: Two Founders, One Decision: Keep Pushing or Stop?
items.author: DL
items.content:
Both stalled on direction. One stopped; the other chose a narrower test.

Two founders, both stuck, both confronting whether to continue. Different years, but the same underlying question. One shut his company down. One decided to keep going. On the evidence each had, both decisions were defensible.

The first founder ran a SaaS for three years and generated $412K in total revenue. Peak MRR was $18K; by the end, it had fallen to $6.2K. He had spent $48K on marketing across ads, content, and agencies. Nothing was dramatically wrong — which is exactly what made the decision hard. His own summary: "Just slow realization that the market was too small and the growth too slow. At $18K MRR peak I could see the ceiling."

He closed it gracefully, helped customers migrate, and closed the accounting with "Still worth it" — the lessons, he wrote, were worth more than what he could have earned working for someone else.

 The second founder was two years into a product with under 100 users and no revenue — he'd switched to free four months in. He'd rewritten the landing page ten times, done six months of outreach, and finally posted the question raw: "Does my product suck? Or is it me?" The top comment in the thread diagnosed it in one line: "Your website is speaking to everyone and no one in particular." He decided to give it another six months and test a more focused marketing approach.

From a distance, both look like "should I quit?" Up close, they were different questions entirely.

The first founder was answering: is this market big enough to justify the next four years of my life? He had three years of data, a ceiling he could name, and a market he had measured from the inside. The signals he trusted — the growth curve flattening at a number he could name, a market measured from the inside, and his own answer to whether he'd raise capital for it — pointed the same way. For him, stopping wasn't failure; it was the first decision in years that wasn't deferred.

The second founder was answering: has this direction actually been tested yet? And the honest answer was no. He had never aimed the product at one specific group of people. Ten rewrites of a page that speaks to everyone is not ten experiments — it's one experiment run ten times. The commenters saw it instantly. You can't read "no product-market fit" off a sample that was never shown to a defined market.

That's the distinction most "should I kill it" threads miss: sometimes the stall is information, and sometimes the stall is just missing data.

How to Tell Which One You're In

There is no clean formula that removes the trade-offs. But two questions separate the cases better than most metrics:

First: has the direction been tested at full strength — aimed at one named audience, with an offer built for them, long enough for them to respond? If not, the stall is weak evidence about product-market fit. That was founder two. That six-month window would have been his first focused test.

Second: if something important hasn't been tried yet, what is the wait buying? The current 33-case public index — stalled-product postmortems classified by failure layer — shows direction problems as the single largest layer at 28%, and not one case was purely a funnel problem. The index is, among other things, a record of founders who left that question unresolved in public.

Evidence That Can Answer Different Questions

One more distinction, because it matters: different evidence answers different questions. Views, upvotes, waitlist signups, and kind words show attention — and attention alone can't answer a keep-or-stop question. A real payment proves one buyer existed, once. A renewal starts to say something about the product.

What buyers say when they specifically decline answers a question traffic never will. None of these decides anything by itself — and neither decision above could have been made from attention alone.

If your direction has been tested at full strength and the ceiling is visible — the way founder one could name his at $18K MRR — stopping is not the failure state. Dragging out a decided question is.

And if it hasn't been tested — if you've been marketing to everyone, the way founder two was — then "should I kill it" is the wrong question, and the honest answer is you don't know yet. Narrow first. Aim at one audience. Then let the stall talk.

Direction problems don't all end in shutdowns. Sometimes they end in a smaller, sharper product. The skill isn't deciding to stop or to persist — it's knowing which situation you're actually in.

The two postmortems are public — three-year SaaS shutdown ($412K): reddit.com/r/SaaS/comments/1rpa3d7/ and "Does my product suck? Or is it me?": indiehackers.com/post/does-my-product-suck-or-is-it-me-82be9149ec.

items.title: Journalists Ignore Most Press Releases: Here's Why
items.author: Vipin Labroo
items.content:
Why do journalists ignore most press releases? The simple answer is that there have always been way too many, and AI slop has only compounded the problem recently. According to a 2025 survey, 90 percent of the press releases disseminated to journalists are not found to be newsworthy, so is it any surprise that journalists reject them?

That being stated, press releases remain a tried and tested method of informing journalists of developments in any realm of the world, ranging from business and brands to entertainment, healthcare, politics and society. It is the thoughtless and reckless mass dissemination based on the spray-and-pray principle that puts journalists off this sometimes important instrument of media engagement.

Thoughtless distribution of press releases is akin to a candidate guessing their way through a multiple-choice, high-stakes entrance examination with negative marking. It never ends well.

In fact, there is a whole set of factors that are responsible for journalists ignoring a press release. Let us look at what these might be:

1. Not targeting the right beat.

Targeting the right beat should be basic knowledge for any PR professional, but you would be surprised how many of them send out press releases across beats, without realising how counterproductive that is. Imagine a healthcare journalist receiving a press release about the launch of a new sports car! Wouldn't that put them off press releases altogether?

2. Focusing on your product and not the journalist’s audience.

Getting your client’s product or service coverage may be your priority as a PR person, but the journalist’s priority is to provide their reader, listener or viewer with information that is useful to the latter. If you want your press release to be part of the less than 50 percent of the traditional press releases that are used by media houses, you better get this right.

So you have to be subtle in the way that you convey that information to the journalists. If your press release is about a restaurant launch, instead of going ga ga over its name and impending date of opening, it might interest the journalist to learn about the target market of the outlet, its cuisine, the number of people it can seat, the size of its staff and other such information which the journalist might use to develop a story.

​3. Not customizing your press release.

When you buy a car, you carry out research about which car caters to your specific requirements. Likewise, if you buy a house, you take your time in evaluating your options before zeroing in on the right one.

Similarly, when you start creating a press release to pitch to journalists across media outlets, you have to be aware of not only their beat, but also the kind of subjects that interest them. It makes eminent sense for you to prepare a bespoke pitch that speaks to their requirement.

If you, for instance, know a journalist who specializes in analyzing the financial results of a company, you should send them something appropriate and not something to do with an unrelated topic like the CSR milestones achieved by the former.

4. The losing relevance of the press release.

The traditional press release is increasingly losing relevance in the digital era, which is more and more about real-time news. Unlike in the past, before social media upended everything, press releases were a vital source of information and news. Not so any longer. Today, there are a myriad of news and information sources ranging from social media feeds to websites. Probably very few media people view press releases as a primary conduit of news and information in these times. So, there is less and less incentive to consult a press release for news these days.

Press releases are always going to be around as a formal document for notifying the media about something pertaining to the company in question. For instance, you may want to inform them about a company’s financial results or announcement or a product launch.

But their days as a dynamic medium of information and news are largely over. A tweet can express the meat of a press release to a journalist in an instant. The latter’s usefulness is limited to providing the details pertaining to product specifications, facts, figures, and other such details.

Why would they wade through an almost archaic document that provides them with dated insights to stay on top of information and news that their audience wants in real time? Clearly, the best days of press releases are behind them.

items.title: People Training OpenAI's AI Fired For Using AI To Train the AI
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
404 Media reports "multiple contractors hired to improve OpenAI's models have been fired for using AI to train the AI:

That's not great for the models themselves, but there is also obviously a great irony in AI training companies working for OpenAI firing people for using AI when OpenAI's whole thing is to make people use AI at work... OpenAI declined to comment on its contractors being fired for using AI. 

Their article cites internal documents and three contractors working on OpenAI-related projects which can include more than ten thousand contractors:

One contractor said they see people using AI "all the time and people are let go for it all the time, it's pretty much the one thing that will get you kicked off ASAP." The person said, "in a group of thousands there are tons that have been caught...." Two of the sources said people have been fired or offboarded for using AI... One contractor said they used AI while helping to train OpenAI's models and shared what they presented as their termination letter. It said their employer had identified issues with the "authenticity" of their work.... 

404 Media spoke to a fourth contractor who has worked on training models for various AI companies. They said they sometimes purposefully chose the worst responses because they wanted to actively sabotage the models' training. "I did feel guilty about doing this kind of work at the start," they said. "I either pay zero attention to the results and choose randomly or purposely choose the [worst] output. I'm not sure how much of a difference it actually makes since there are hundreds of other people also rating prompt results, but it does feel like I'm getting paid to make AI worse."
 

Two of the contractors worked for Mercor, the article reports, a company which last month Nvidia reportedly discussed funding at a $20 billion valuation. 



Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the article.

items.title: What is a DAG-Based Cryptocurrency - and Why It Matters
items.author: Obyte
items.content:
The term “blockchain technology” is overused now, and its definition has become diffuse, in the best of cases. We tend to associate it with anything related to cryptocurrencies, or that uses their underlying technology, but the truth is that a blockchain, as such, is just one type of structure that cryptocurrencies can use as a building block. Other structures exist, like the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

We can’t say one structure is better than the other, but they pursue different goals and offer different things. Let’s learn a bit about this.

How Does a DAG-Based Cryptocurrency Work?

As its name suggests, a ‘block-chain’ records transactions inside “blocks” of data that are added one after another in strict chronological order. They have different ways to reach consensus to ‘approve’ transactions; the most popular ones being with miners (Proof-of-Work/PoW) or “validators” (Proof-of-Stake/PoS). Bitcoin and Ethereum are blockchains. DAG-based cryptocurrencies, like , are blockchains at all.

Instead of blocks, we can say that a DAG builds a huge net of interconnected transactions. Before joining the ledger, a new transaction connects to one or more earlier ones, creating a web of links that expands over time. Each user is “their own miner,” as Sergio Demian Lerner, the first one to describe a DAG-based cryptocurrency, .

“DagCoin is a cryptocurrency design that attempts to be highly decentralized by merging the concepts of transactions and blocks and making each user that transact a miner. Each transaction carries a proof-of-work and references one or more previous transactions. The resulting authenticated data structure is a Direct Acyclic Graph (DAG) of transactions where each transaction “confirms” one or more previous transactions.”

Of course, this was just an initial concept, and different DAG networks have applied it with different changes. describes the way information is organized, but it doesn't dictate how participants agree on valid transactions. Every project builds its own rules.

Obyte, for instance, is a DAG ledger built by its own users. Every user adds their own transactions to the ledger, and no one can stop them — ensuring the maximum possible decentralization. To establish chronological order of transactions, which are already in the ledger, Obyte has a group of (OPs). They don’t have any other power.

Other DAG tokens use different methods, so there's no universal blueprint. Decentralization also depends on those methods.

Why Does This Design Matter?

New designs and protocols always matter in the crypto world, for a start. In a DAG-based system, transactions can form a graph of relationships, where multiple transactions can be added without all of them needing to fit into one single sequence. Some projects choose a DAG-like structure trying to increase throughput, while Obyte chooses it for the ultimate .

This is an important feature: the more decentralized a crypto network is, the more resistant it is to potential censorship and manipulation.Blockchains are decentralized to a degree, considering that anyone with the right equipment, knowledge, and/or enough funds can become a miner or “validator” to help approve transactions and receive rewards in exchange. Still, these miners or validators can be considered powerhouses or central parties by themselves. In some bad cases, they can even . On the other hand, DAG-based crypto networks offer various consensus methods, with different levels of decentralization for each one.

Some of them still have central parties or pre-selected, to order or approve transactions, which can lead to centralization. Obyte isn’t like that: every user is its own “miner.” This design matters because they add transactions themselves, directly, without middlemen, without gatekeepers, and nobody can stop them. This way, Obyte is a truly decentralized, unstoppable network, available for everyone, everywhere.

For newcomers, the biggest takeaway is simple: Cryptocurrency isn't built around one fixed recipe. Blockchain may dominate the headlines, yet alternatives continue to expand the field with fresh ideas. That diversity gives developers more tools to work with and gives users more options when choosing the technology that best fits their needs.
